rv.q: It deserves more drama, emotion and political complexity on the ground.
Whilst it isn’t perfect, Safe Haven proves that not everything has to be fluff to prove entertaining, and not everything informative has to be didactic and force-fed.
For all its faults, there’s a good play poking through the flawed one we see, but there’s a fair bit of surgery still required to ensure that it blossoms.
In these dark days, a must-see.
The text stands confidently on its own, supported by the cast’s performances rather than interesting staging or directorial conception.
Perhaps the clumsiness in the script was unavoidable.
Ultimately, it cannot go unfelt that there is an element of the ‘white saviour’ trope that sits uncomfortably in the driver’s seat.
However, the play’s focus on diplomatic manoeuvring over refugee experience means it falls flat.

cn.t: Bowers' debut play about the 1991 Kurdish crisis divides critics. While his diplomatic insider knowledge brings authenticity, the production struggles with didactic dialogue and fails to fully captivate despite its powerful subject matter.
